t: Maximum Score of a Split — Prefix Sums + Suffix Minima
o: We must pick a split index i (0 <= i < n-1) maximizing prefixSum(i) - suffixMin(i), where the prefix is nums[0..i] and the suffix minimum covers nums[i+1..n-1]. In Example 1, i=2 gives (10-1+3) - (-5) = 17. In Example 2, only i=0 or i=1 are valid; i=0 gives -7-(-5) = -2, which beats i=1 (-12-3). With n up to 1e5, an O(n^2) recomputation of sums and minima per split would be ~1e10 operations — too slow, so we need precomputation to answer each split in O(1).
k: Precompute prefix sums left-to-right and suffix minima right-to-left in one pass each.
score(i) = prefixSum(i) - suffixMin(i) can then be evaluated in O(1) for every valid i.
Values can be as large as 1e9 * 1e5, so use 64-bit integers.

a.i: For every split index i, directly compute the prefix sum by looping over nums[0..i] and the suffix minimum by looping over nums[i+1..n-1], then take the maximum score. This is straightforward but quadratic.
s: For each i from 0 to n-2: sum nums[0..i] into p.
a.t: O(n^2) — for each of the n-1 splits we rescan both sides.

a.i: Both quantities needed at index i depend only on position: prefixSum(i) is a running total updated incrementally, and suffixMin(i) can be built once by scanning from the right. Precomputing both arrays lets us evaluate all splits in a single final pass. This reduces the work to three linear passes.
s: Build sufMin where sufMin[i] = min(nums[i..n-1]) via a right-to-left scan.
Initialize running prefix sum p = 0 and best = negative infinity.
For i from 0 to n-2: add nums[i] to p.
a.t: O(n) — two linear passes build the suffix minima and evaluate all splits.
a.sp: O(n) for the suffix-minimum array (could be O(1) if you fold the right-to-left min into the main loop).

w: In an interview, mention the brute force briefly, then present the O(n) prefix-sum/suffix-min solution as the answer. Pitfalls: forgetting that i ranges only to n-2 (the suffix must be non-empty), off-by-one when indexing sufMin[i+1], and integer overflow — with n=1e5 and values up to 1e9 the score reaches ~1e14, so use long/long long (Python ints are safe). Edge cases: n=2 (single split), all-negative arrays (answer may still be negative), and large positive values after a very negative suffix element. A likely follow-up: achieve O(1) extra space by maintaining the suffix min on the fly while iterating i from n-2 down to 0 alongside a precomputed total prefix sum.
